hints: Look closely at the bottom diagram in Fig. 2.1 at 1.5 nm scale - what shape is each single strand and how do the three strands sit together?
Think about the special name given when three helical polypeptides wind tightly around a common axis.
walkthrough:
See Each Single Chain**
Each of the three polypeptides is itself coiled into a helix. In collagen this is a left-handed helix, which is different from the right-handed alpha-helix found in many globular proteins.

See How Three Wind Together**
The three helical chains then wind tightly around each other, like a three-stranded rope. This combined structure is called the triple helix, which gives the collagen molecule its great strength.
Final answer: Each polypeptide is a left-handed helix. The three polypeptides are tightly coiled around each other to form a triple helix.

hints: Look at the middle fibril diagram in Fig. 2.1 - are the short lines representing molecules lined up end-to-end or side-by-side, and do their ends line up?
Think about what type of strong bond must link separate molecules together to give high tensile strength, not just the hydrogen bonds within the triple helix.
Recall where cross-links form between different polypeptide chains - which part of the amino acid is involved?
walkthrough:
Parallel Packing**
In a fibril, many 300 nm long collagen molecules lie side by side with all their long axes pointing the same way. That is a parallel arrangement.

Staggered Overlap**
They are not lined up end-to-end like bricks in a perfect wall. They overlap in a staggered way, so the end of one molecule is beside the middle of the next. You can see this offset pattern in the fibril in Fig. 2.1. This staggering spreads load and adds strength.

Covalent Cross-links Hold Them**
Hydrogen bonds hold the three chains inside one molecule, but different molecules in the fibril are linked by much stronger covalent bonds. These form between the R-groups (side chains) of amino acids on neighbouring molecules, for example between lysine residues.

Final answer: Collagen molecules are arranged in parallel and staggered so ends are not aligned. Molecules are held together by covalent bonds between R-groups of amino acids on different molecules, e.g. between lysine residues.

hints: Think about what would happen to a soft tube when air pressure drops during inhalation - what mechanical property stops it collapsing?
Think about why the trachea cannot be a rigid pipe - it must bend with neck movement and change diameter slightly during breathing.
walkthrough:
Strength To Hold Airway Open**
Cartilage C-rings in the trachea wall contain collagen fibres. Collagen has very high tensile strength, so it resists pulling forces and supports the wall. This keeps the trachea open so air can flow freely and stops it collapsing when pressure falls on inhalation.

Flexibility For Movement**
Collagen fibres are strong but can also allow a degree of flexibility. This lets the trachea bend with the neck, and stretch slightly to allow small changes in diameter during ventilation, without breaking.

Final answer: Collagen provides high tensile strength to support the trachea and keep the airway open / prevent collapse. It also allows flexibility for breathing movements and bending of the trachea.

hints: Think about what alveoli walls must do on inhalation when they fill with air, and then do passively on exhalation.
walkthrough:
Stretch and Recoil**
Elastic fibres can stretch easily when alveoli inflate on inhalation without tearing, then recoil elastically. Recoil squeezes the alveoli and helps push air out on exhalation.
Final answer: Allow stretching / expansion without rupture on inhalation and recoil to help expel air on exhalation.

hints: Remember the non-transcribed strand has the same sequence as mRNA except T replaces U, so you can read its triplets directly in Table 2.2, starting with GGT.
walkthrough:
Read The Coding Strand**
The non-transcribed strand is the coding strand. Its triplets GGT, CCA, ATG, GGT, CCC, CGA, GGT, CCC, CCA, GGT correspond to mRNA codons GGU, CCA, AUG, etc. Using Table 2.2: GGT = gly, CCA / CCC = pro, ATG = met, CGA = arg. This gives gly-pro-met-gly-pro-arg-gly-pro-pro-gly.

hints: Look at the pattern in your answer to (c)(i) - which amino acid appears in position 1, 4, 7 and 10?
Think about the size of that repeating amino acid compared with all others and why small size matters inside a tightly wound triple helix.
Think about how the backbone -NH and -CO groups of closely packed chains can interact to stabilise the helix.
walkthrough:
Spot The Repeat**
Your sequence shows gly-X-Y-gly-X-Y. Glycine occurs at every third position. This Gly-X-Y repeat is representative of the whole collagen polypeptide.

Small Size Allows Tight Fit**
Glycine is the smallest amino acid because its R-group is just a single hydrogen atom. Only such a tiny side chain can fit into the crowded centre of the triple helix where the three chains touch. Any larger R-group would push the chains apart.

Stability Through Hydrogen Bonds**
Because the chains can pack so closely, the -NH group of glycine can form hydrogen bonds with -CO groups on a neighbouring chain. With glycine at every third position, many hydrogen bonds form along the whole length, locking the triple helix together.

Final answer: Glycine is every third amino acid. Glycine has the smallest R-group (H) so polypeptides can fit closely together / fold tightly. The close packing allows many hydrogen bonds between polypeptides, stabilising the triple helix.

hints: Think about what happens to the triplet reading frame if you remove one nucleotide from the start versus if you just swap one base for another.
Think about how many codons downstream are affected in each case - all of them or just the one where the change occurred?
walkthrough:
P Is A Frameshift Deletion**
Primary structure means the order of amino acids. Deleting one nucleotide pair shifts the whole triplet reading frame. Every codon after the deletion is read differently, so the entire amino acid sequence downstream changes.

Q Is A Single Missense Substitution**
Substituting G with T in the first triplet changes GGT to TGT on the coding strand. TGT codes for cys instead of gly. Because triplets are still read in the same frame, only that first codon is altered and all later amino acids stay the same.

Final answer: Mutation P (deletion of first nucleotide): changes the sequence / order of amino acids in the whole primary structure downstream (frameshift). Mutation Q (substitution of G with T in first triplet): only the first amino acid changes to cys instead of gly, rest of sequence unchanged.
